writing.scenario: Your English penfriend Liam wants to visit your city next month. Write him an email.
taskRequirements: Suggest the best place to visit in your city and say why.
Tell him what kind of weather to expect.
Offer to meet him at the airport or train station.
writing.modelAnswer:
Hi Liam,
I am so excited that you are visiting next month! You should definitely visit the Old Town because the architecture and street cafés are amazing. The weather is usually cool and rainy in autumn, so bring a warm jacket. Send me your arrival time and I will happily meet you at the train station!
Best,
Alex

speaking.title: Speaking · Comparing Everyday Activities
bulletPoints: How do you usually travel for holidays?
What do you like or dislike about train travel?
Describe a fun trip you took last year (Past Simple).
speaking.followUpQuestion: Would you rather visit a big capital city or a quiet mountain village?
speaking.modelResponseScript: I usually prefer travelling by train because I can read a book, drink coffee, and watch the countryside without worrying about traffic. Last year I went to Edinburgh by train with two friends. We walked up Arthur’s Seat, ate fish and chips, and had a fantastic weekend.

reading.title: Reading · Magazine Feature & Inference
reading.passageTitle: Why Silent Book Clubs Are Spreading Worldwide
reading.passage: Traditional book clubs often make busy adults feel guilty: if you fail to finish the chosen novel on time, you dread showing up to the meeting. Silent Book Clubs flip that formula on its head. Members gather at a local café or library, spend twenty minutes chatting about whatever book they happen to be reading, and then read silently together for a full hour. There is no assigned reading list and no pressure to produce brilliant literary commentary—just shared quiet focus in a distracted world.

questions.prompt: Why do some people avoid traditional book clubs according to the article?
options: They feel stressed if they do not finish the assigned book on time.
They prefer audiobooks over paper books.
questions.explanation: "if you fail to finish the chosen novel on time, you dread showing up to the meeting."

questions.prompt: What happens during the main hour of a Silent Book Club meetup?
options: Members debate one assigned classic novel.
Everyone reads their own chosen book quietly together.
An author reads a chapter aloud.
questions.explanation: Members read whatever book they brought silently together for a full hour.

questions.prompt: What does "flip that formula on its head" mean here?
questions.explanation: Idiomatic phrasing meaning to invert or radically redesign the conventional model.

listening.title: Listening & Hearing · Podcast Interview (Connected Speech)
listening.contextNote: Listen to a short podcast clip about urban cycling infrastructure.
listening.audioScript: Host: So when Copenhagen started expanding its protected bike lanes, did drivers push back at first? Guest: Oh, absolutely—local merchants worried customers wouldn’t turn up if street parking disappeared. Yet within two years, foot and cycle traffic rose so sharply that neighborhood bakery and café revenues actually went up. People stop far more spontaneously when they’re on a bike than when they’re hunting for a parking spot.
listening.hearingFocusTrap: Hear phrasal verbs ("push back", "turn up", "went up") and contrast initial merchant fear vs. 2-year reality.

questions.prompt: What were local shopkeepers initially worried about?
options: Losing customers because of fewer street parking spaces
questions.explanation: "local merchants worried customers wouldn’t turn up if street parking disappeared."

questions.prompt: What actually happened to café and bakery revenues within two years?
questions.explanation: "revenues actually went up."

questions.prompt: Why does the guest say cyclists spend more at neighborhood shops?
options: Cyclists can stop spontaneously without searching for parking.
questions.explanation: "People stop far more spontaneously when they’re on a bike than when they’re hunting for a parking spot."

writing.title: Writing · B1 Preliminary Article (100–130 Words)
writing.scenario: An international student magazine asks readers to write an article titled: "Learning a Language Outside the Classroom."
taskRequirements: Describe two practical ways to learn a language outside formal lessons.
Explain which method worked best for you and why.
Include at least two phrasal verbs or linking words (although, however, because, figure out).
writing.modelAnswer: Although grammar textbooks give you a useful starting map, real fluency usually begins outside the classroom. Two of the most effective habits I have discovered are listening to daily podcasts during my commute and shadowing short video clips aloud. At first, native speakers sounded far too fast; however, once I started listening to topics I genuinely enjoyed—like cooking and travel—my comprehension jumped dramatically. For me, speaking for ten minutes a day with language partners worked best because it forced me to figure out how to express real ideas under pressure. If you make the language part of your hobbies, studying stops feeling like homework.

speaking.title: Speaking · B1 Topic Talk & Decision
speaking.cueCardTitle: Working from Home vs. Working in an Office
bulletPoints: Main advantages of working remotely
Challenges people face when they rarely see colleagues in person
Which setup you would choose and why
speaking.followUpQuestion: Do you think most jobs will stay hybrid over the next ten years?
speaking.modelResponseScript: Working from home saves a huge amount of commuting time and makes it easier to focus on deep tasks without office noise. However, staying completely remote can feel isolating, especially when you need quick feedback from colleagues. Personally, I would choose a hybrid schedule—three days at home and two days in the office—because it combines quiet productivity with genuine team connection.

reading.title: Reading · IELTS Academic Passage (Inference & T/F/NG)
reading.passageTitle: The Paradox of Urban Tree Canopies
reading.passage: Expanding urban tree cover is widely celebrated as one of the most cost-effective defenses against extreme summer heatwaves, lowering neighborhood surface temperatures by up to four degrees Celsius. Yet urban ecologists emphasize that planting millions of saplings carelessly can backfire. In arid regions, selecting water-hungry non-native species strains municipal aquifers, while planting monocultures leaves entire avenues vulnerable to a single pest outbreak. Resilient greening therefore hinges not on raw tree counts, but on biodiverse, drought-adapted native species paired with soil volume large enough for mature roots.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why can planting a single tree species across a city backfire?
options: It provides less shade than mixed species.
It leaves whole streets exposed to a single pest outbreak.
It raises summer surface temperatures by four degrees.
It prevents residents from walking on sidewalks.
questions.explanation: "planting monocultures leaves entire avenues vulnerable to a single pest outbreak."

questions.prompt: TRUE, FALSE, or NOT GIVEN: "The passage states that urban tree planting is more expensive than air-conditioning subsidies."
questions.explanation: Air-conditioning subsidies are never mentioned anywhere in the text -> NOT GIVEN (classic IELTS trap!).

questions.prompt: What determines resilient urban greening according to ecologists?
options: Maximizing the total raw number of saplings planted each year
Biodiverse, drought-adapted native species with adequate soil volume
Importing fast-growing tropical trees into arid cities
Replacing all paved roads with parks
questions.explanation: The closing sentence directly states resilient greening hinges on biodiverse, drought-adapted native species and sufficient soil volume.

listening.title: Listening & Hearing · Academic Seminar (IELTS Part 3)
listening.contextNote: Listen to two university students comparing study strategies before finals.
listening.audioScript: Maya: I used to spend hours highlighting textbook chapters in neon yellow, thinking I was absorbing everything. Leo: Same here—until I bombed a mock exam and realized passive rereading creates an illusion of competence. Switching to active recall flashcards and explaining concepts aloud to an empty room cut my revision time almost in half. Maya: That’s exactly what I’m trying this semester, though spacing reviews over weeks instead of cramming is the hardest habit to stick to.
listening.hearingFocusTrap: Track the distinction between "illusion of competence" (highlighting) and Maya’s toughest obstacle (spacing over weeks).

questions.prompt: What mistake did both Maya and Leo make previously?
options: Relying on passive highlighting and rereading
Revising too early in the semester
questions.explanation: Maya highlighted chapters and Leo agrees passive rereading created an "illusion of competence".

questions.prompt: How did active recall affect Leo’s preparation?
options: It nearly halved his revision time.
It caused him to fail his mock exam.
questions.explanation: "cut my revision time almost in half."

questions.prompt: What does Maya find most challenging now?
options: Consistently spacing her reviews over weeks instead of cramming
questions.explanation: "spacing reviews over weeks instead of cramming is the hardest habit to stick to."

writing.title: Writing · IELTS Task 2 / FCE Opinion Essay (160–240 Words)
writing.scenario: Some educators argue that students should learn practical financial and digital literacy at school instead of spending years studying a foreign language. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
taskRequirements: Present a clear thesis statement in your introduction.
Develop two well-supported body paragraphs addressing both sides.
Use natural B2 collocations and cohesive discourse markers (however, furthermore, nevertheless, on the other hand).
writing.modelAnswer:
As modern economies become increasingly digitized, many argue that schools should replace mandatory foreign language classes with financial and digital literacy. While equipping teenagers with practical life skills is undeniably vital, treating these subjects as mutually exclusive is a false dichotomy.

On the one hand, understanding compound interest, budgeting, and digital privacy protects young adults from costly real-world mistakes. Schools have historically overlooked these competencies, leaving graduates underprepared for adult independence. However, eliminating language education would strip students of far more than vocabulary lists. Learning another tongue strengthens cognitive flexibility, deepens cultural empathy, and opens international career opportunities that translation software cannot replicate.

Furthermore, technology already allows schools to integrate financial projects into mathematics and digital ethics into civics without sacrificing humanities. In conclusion, rather than pitting practical literacy against linguistic mastery, modern curricula should balance both so graduates are financially resilient and globally connected.

speaking.title: Speaking · IELTS Part 2 Cue Card + Part 3 Follow-Up
speaking.cueCardTitle: Describe a Challenging Goal You Achieved
bulletPoints: What the goal was and why it mattered to you
The biggest obstacle you encountered along the way
How you overcame it and what you learned about yourself
speaking.followUpQuestion: Why do you think many people abandon ambitious long-term goals after the first month?
speaking.modelResponseScript: A challenging goal I achieved was reaching conversational fluency in German while working full time. Initially, I underestimated how intimidating case endings and fast native speech would be, and after two months I hit a frustrating plateau. However, instead of giving up, I redesigned my routine around twenty minutes of daily shadowing and weekly speaking sessions. Eventually, conversations stopped feeling like math puzzles, and the experience taught me that small daily systems outperform occasional bursts of motivation.

reading.title: Reading · Academic Policy Critique (C1 Inference)
reading.passageTitle: The Metrics Trap in Preventive Healthcare
reading.passage: Wearable biosensors promise to shift medicine from reactive treatment to continuous prevention, empowering individuals to track heart-rate variability, sleep architecture, and blood glucose in real time. Yet clinicians caution that ubiquitous self-tracking is a double-edged sword. For patients managing chronic conditions, timely trend alerts can genuinely avert hospitalizations. Conversely, among otherwise healthy users, hyper-vigilant monitoring of noisy physiological fluctuations frequently breeds unnecessary anxiety and drives low-value clinical visits—diverting scarce diagnostic capacity away from underserved populations who lack basic primary care altogether.

questions.prompt: Why do clinicians describe wearable biosensors as a "double-edged sword"?
options: They are accurate for sleep tracking but fail for heart rate.
They benefit chronic-care patients yet can trigger anxiety and misallocate healthcare capacity among healthy users.
They are too expensive for hospitals to purchase.
They replace primary care physicians entirely.
questions.explanation: The text contrasts genuine preventive gains for chronic patients against anxiety and resource diversion caused by healthy hyper-vigilant users.

questions.prompt: What systemic equity concern is raised at the end of the passage?
options: Low-value visits by worried healthy users consume capacity needed by underserved communities.
Clinicians refuse to inspect wearable metrics.
questions.explanation: "diverting scarce diagnostic capacity away from underserved populations who lack basic primary care altogether."

questions.prompt: Which word best matches "noisy physiological fluctuations" in context?
questions.explanation: In data/clinical usage, "noisy fluctuations" refers to harmless background variance rather than meaningful pathology.

listening.title: Listening & Hearing · Single-Play University Lecture (TOEFL/CAE)
listening.contextNote: Strict C1 Mode: You hear this behavioral economics lecture excerpt ONLY ONCE.
listening.audioScript: One of the most counterintuitive findings in behavioral economics is the paradox of choice. Classical rational-actor models assumed that expanding options could only improve welfare—after all, you can simply ignore alternatives you dislike. Yet field experiments repeatedly reveal that when shoppers face twenty-four varieties of jam instead of six, conversion rates actually plummet. Evaluating excessive options imposes cognitive overload and amplifies anticipated regret: even after choosing, consumers nag themselves wondering whether one of the rejected options might have been marginally superior.
listening.hearingFocusTrap: Single play only! Connect "classical assumption" vs. "jam field experiment" -> "cognitive overload + anticipated regret".

questions.prompt: What assumption of classical economics is challenged by the jam experiment?
options: That adding more options invariably increases consumer welfare and buying
questions.explanation: Classical models assumed expanding options only improves welfare, whereas 24 varieties caused conversion rates to plummet.

questions.prompt: What two psychological mechanisms explain the drop in purchases?
questions.explanation: The lecturer explicitly names "cognitive overload" and "anticipated regret".

questions.prompt: How does excessive choice affect consumers AFTER they make a purchase?
options: They worry a rejected alternative might have been slightly better.
questions.explanation: "consumers nag themselves wondering whether one of the rejected options might have been marginally superior."

writing.title: Writing · CAE / IELTS Band 8 Analytical Essay (220+ Words)
writing.scenario: Write an analytical essay evaluating the statement: "Algorithmic recommendation systems expand cultural horizons far less than they reinforce existing tastes."
taskRequirements: Incorporate at least one stylistic inversion (e.g., Rarely have..., Not only do...) and nuanced hedging (albeit, notwithstanding, to a certain extent).
Weigh both discovery benefits and filter-bubble risks with concrete examples.
Conclude with a measured synthesis.
writing.modelAnswer:
Rarely have cultural gatekeepers wielded as subtle an influence as modern algorithmic recommendation engines. Designed to maximize sustained engagement across music, film, and journalism, these systems undeniably democratize access to niche creators who would previously have struggled for distribution. Nevertheless, their commercial architecture tends to privilege frictionless familiarity over genuine intellectual surprise.

To a certain extent, collaborative filtering does foster serendipitous discovery, connecting listeners with independent artists across continents. However, because retention metrics penalize user drop-off, algorithms overwhelmingly extrapolate from past clicks—serving incrementally safer variations of established preferences. Consequently, audiences risk mistaking an abundance of tailored content for genuine breadth of perspective, albeit within an invisible echo chamber.

Notwithstanding these structural incentives, the remedy lies neither in abandoning digital curation nor in romanticizing legacy media monopolies. Introducing deliberate "diversity dials" alongside human editorial curation could preserve convenient discovery while restoring the creative friction necessary for cultural growth.

speaking.title: Speaking · C1 Abstract Persuasion & Rebuttal
speaking.cueCardTitle: Should Cities Invest More in Cultural Landmarks or Everyday Public Spaces?
bulletPoints: Compare the symbolic/economic draw of iconic landmarks against neighborhood parks & libraries
Explain how investment choices shape social cohesion
Address the counterargument that flagship monuments fund local budgets through tourism
speaking.followUpQuestion: To what extent does architectural design influence how citizens interact across generations?
speaking.modelResponseScript: Flagship cultural landmarks undeniably place a city on the global map and attract tourism revenue. Having said that, civic vitality is forged primarily in everyday third places—accessible libraries, shaded neighborhood parks, and community sports halls—where residents cross paths regardless of income. Whereas monumental architecture impresses visitors for an afternoon, modest, well-maintained public spaces quietly sustain social cohesion every single day. Ultimately, municipal budgets should prioritize everyday livability first, treating iconic venues as a complement rather than a substitute.

reading.title: Reading · Literary & Philosophical Prose (C2 Nuance)
reading.passage: Contemporary software design treats cognitive friction as an engineering defect to be engineered out of existence. Yet in the domain of human expertise, effortless interfaces harbor a quiet irony: the very struggle that learners instinctively seek to bypass is the biological signal that consolidates durable neural pathways. When an application reduces a rich intellectual discipline to gamified streaks and frictionless taps, it delivers the comforting sensation of progress while subtly insulating the user from the disorienting ambiguity through which authentic fluency is forged.

questions.prompt: What paradox does the author identify in gamified, frictionless learning apps?
options: They are too visually complex for beginners.
By removing productive difficulty, they simulate progress while preventing the cognitive struggle required for real mastery.
They rely too heavily on printed textbooks.
questions.explanation: They deliver "the comforting sensation of progress while subtly insulating the user from the disorienting ambiguity" needed for genuine mastery.

questions.prompt: In the sentence "the very struggle ... is the biological signal", what rhetorical function does "very" serve?
options: It acts as an emphatic determiner highlighting exact identity ("the precise struggle itself").
questions.explanation: "The very [noun]" is a C2 emphatic structure pinpointing exact identity.

questions.prompt: Which tone best characterizes the passage?
questions.explanation: The prose is restrained yet incisive ("quiet irony", "subtly insulating"), characteristic of C2 editorial criticism.

listening.title: Listening & Hearing · Pragmatic Irony & Understatement (Single-Play)
listening.contextNote: Strict C2 Mode: Single play. Listen carefully for British understatement and unspoken critique.
listening.audioScript: Host: Professor Vance, you served on the national curriculum review panel. Were you satisfied with the final compromise? Vance: Let us just say the document is a monument to committee prose—scrupulously polite, wonderfully symmetrical, and almost entirely unburdened by actionable specificity. If one’s goal was to offend nobody at the conference table, it was a roaring success; if one hoped to help an overworked teacher on a rainy Tuesday morning, well, one might wait a little longer.
listening.hearingFocusTrap: Decode ironic praise ("monument to committee prose", "unburdened by actionable specificity", "roaring success").

questions.prompt: What does Professor Vance actually think of the final curriculum document?
options: It is brilliantly structured and immediately helpful to teachers.
It is overly vague and politically cautious, offering little practical help to classroom teachers.
It was far too controversial and offended committee members.
It focused excessively on Tuesday lesson plans.
questions.explanation: "Unburdened by actionable specificity" is classic C2 ironic understatement for "completely vague".

questions.prompt: What does "roaring success" refer to in Vance’s remark?
options: Avoiding diplomatic friction inside the committee rather than solving real classroom needs
questions.explanation: Vance ironically defines its "success" solely as offending nobody at the conference table.

questions.prompt: What is implied by "one might wait a little longer"?
options: A helpful update arrives next week.
Teachers should not expect practical reform from this document anytime soon.
questions.explanation: Dry British litotes implying real change is nowhere in sight.

writing.title: Writing · CPE Evaluative Synthesis Essay (240+ Words)
writing.scenario: Write a C2 evaluative essay addressing the prompt: "Does the relentless pursuit of convenience enrich human agency, or quietly diminish the capacities that make us resilient?"
taskRequirements: Demonstrate effortless command of register, syntactic rhythm, and inverted conditionals (Were societies to..., Had we...).
Synthesize both legitimate gains of modern convenience and subtle cognitive/cultural losses.
Avoid clichés; close with a memorable, incisive formulation.
writing.modelAnswer:
Ostensibly, the history of technological progress is a chronicle of liberation from drudgery. Eliminating arduous manual chores—from hand-washing linen to navigating unfamiliar cities without maps—has unquestionably widened human agency, freeing millions to pursue creative, intellectual, and civic endeavors. Nevertheless, convenience ceases to be benign the moment it begins to outsource not merely physical labor, but the formative disciplines of attention, memory, and judgment.

Were societies to automate every minor cognitive inconvenience, they might discover too late that competence is rarely separable from effort. Just as muscles atrophy without load, intellectual resilience depends on periodic encounters with ambiguity—wrestling with an untranslated text, negotiating a face-to-face disagreement, or enduring the slow incubation of a difficult idea. By smoothing away every trace of resistance, frictionless ecosystems risk trading deep capability for passive dependency.

Ultimately, the test of any convenience should not be how much effort it spares us, but what higher form of engagement it enables. True agency lies not in escaping difficulty altogether, but in choosing which difficulties are worthy of our devotion.

speaking.title: Speaking · CPE Impromptu Philosophical Long Turn
speaking.cueCardTitle: Language as a Lens on Reality
bulletPoints: How acquiring a second or third language reshapes perception, humor, and nuance
Whether a single global lingua franca threatens intellectual diversity
How polyglots can bridge cultural divides in an increasingly polarized world
speaking.followUpQuestion: Is complete translation between two cultures ever truly possible, or is something vital always transformed in transit?
speaking.modelResponseScript: While a shared global lingua franca undeniably accelerates scientific collaboration and commerce, treating language as a mere interchangeable code overlooks its deepest power. Stepping into German syntax or English diplomatic understatement gently rearranges how one frames causality, politeness, and humor. Something subtle is inevitably transformed in translation—not necessarily lost, but refracted through a different cultural prism. Ultimately, cultivating multilingual fluency preserves intellectual humility: it reminds us that our native vocabulary is only one map of human experience, never the territory itself.
